summary: Updates the guidance in RFC 3261, which required 3DES as the mandatory cipher for S/MIME in SIP, to require the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) instead. It is a short change reflecting AES as the stronger and preferred choice.

eli5.summary: This document swaps an older lock for a newer, stronger one in secure phone-call setup messages.

questions: what does rfc 3853 change in rfc 3261
which aes key sizes must sip s/mime support
subtitle: SIP's mandatory S/MIME encryption algorithm changes from 3DES to AES.

tldr.problem: RFC 3261 made 3DES the mandatory encryption algorithm for S/MIME in SIP, while TLS support in SIP already requires AES, so implementations had to carry both.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3853 replaces the fifth bullet of RFC 3261 section 23.3: S/MIME implementations MUST support RSA signatures, SHA1 digests and AES encryption, with 128-bit AES keys required and 192 and 256-bit keys recommended.
tldr.outcome: The S/MIME and TLS algorithm requirements line up. 3DES, DH and DSS drop to RECOMMENDED. The document updates RFC 3261.

today: RFC 3853 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2004 that updates RFC 3261. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Move from 3DES to AES
sections.content:
RFC 3261, the SIP specification, supports S/MIME only as optional (a normative MAY). It named Triple-DES (3DES) as the minimum encryption algorithm. Since then S/MIME and the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) have been revised, and AES has been identified as a content-encryption algorithm.

The RFC says AES is widely believed to be faster than 3DES and comparably secure, with comparatively low memory needs, which suits mobile and embedded SIP devices.
sections.eli5: AES is a newer lock that is faster and small enough to fit on little gadgets like phones.

sections.title: Unifying TLS and S/MIME Requirements
sections.content:
SIP recommends (a normative SHOULD) support for Transport Layer Security, and TLS support in SIP requires AES. So an implementation that supports both TLS and S/MIME had to support both 3DES and AES. A similar duplication existed with DSS as a signature algorithm, because the mandatory TLS ciphersuite used by SIP requires RSA.

The RFC argues that S/MIME had not yet seen widespread deployment in SIP user agents, so the minimum could change without obsoleting any substantial deployment. It also notes that work in the S/MIME working group was still in progress and that this document would keep tracking it.
sections.eli5: Before, you needed two different locks to be safe in two situations. Now one kind of lock covers both, which is less to carry.

sections.title: The New Ciphersuite Requirement
sections.content:
The RFC replaces the fifth bullet in section 23.3 of RFC 3261. S/MIME implementations MUST at a minimum support:

  • RSA as a digital signature algorithm and SHA1 as a digest algorithm.
  • AES as an encryption algorithm.
  • RSA key transport, as in section 4.2.1 of its reference [5].

AES implementations MUST support 128-bit keys and SHOULD support 192 and 256-bit keys. The S/MIME specification itself mandates 3DES, DH and DSS, but in the SIP profile support for these is RECOMMENDED and not required. All other signature and encryption algorithms MAY be supported, and implementations can negotiate using the SMIMECapabilities attribute.
sections.eli5: Everyone must know the new lock with a standard-size key. The old locks are nice to have, but not required.

sections.title: Content-Transfer-Encoding
sections.content: SIP is 8-bit clean, so all implementations MUST use 8-bit binary Content-Transfer-Encoding for S/MIME in SIP. Implementations MAY also be able to receive base-64 Content-Transfer-Encoding.
sections.eli5: SIP can carry raw bytes without turning them into letters first, so it sends them as they are. It can still read the lettered form if someone sends it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The migration of the S/MIME requirement from Triple-DES to AES is not known to introduce any new security considerations. The RFC says nothing further on security.
sections.eli5: Trading the old lock for the new one is not expected to open any new doors for bad guys.
